```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(hexmap)
library(sf)
library(ggplot2)
```

The examples use the Australian federal electoral divisions from the ozmaps package, without offshore territories, and the state of each division:

```{r data, warning = FALSE}
ced <- st_crop(ozmaps::abs_ced, xmin = 112, ymin = -44, xmax = 154, ymax = -9)
states <- ozmaps::abs_ste
names(states)[1] <- "state"
ced <- st_join(st_make_valid(ced), st_make_valid(states), largest = TRUE)
```

```{r helpers, include = FALSE}
library(patchwork)
hex_map <- function(hex, crs = st_crs(hex), title = NULL) {
  ggplot(hex) +
    geom_sf(aes(fill = state), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.1,
            show.legend = FALSE) +
    coord_sf(crs = crs) +
    labs(title = title) +
    theme_void() +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 10))
}
```

A hexagon map is drawn on a flat surface, but the regions it represents lie on the curved surface of the Earth. The projection that flattens the Earth decides two things about the hexagons:

* whether they look **regular**, with six equal sides, and
* whether they cover **equal areas on the ground**.

`hexmap()` makes regular, equally sized hexagons in the plane of a projected coordinate reference system (CRS). This is the CRS of the map, or the one given with `crs`. A map in longitude and latitude has no plane to make hexagons in, so by default it is projected with the Lambert azimuthal equal-area projection centred on the map, and a message names the CRS chosen. The hexagons are ordinary `sf` polygons, so they keep their location on the Earth and can be plotted with `geom_sf()` in any projection. They only look regular when plotted in the projection they were made in, and only cover equal areas on the ground when that projection is equal-area.

```{r albers}
ced_hex <- hexmap(ced, group = state, crs = 3577)
ggplot(ced_hex) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = state))
```

## Plotting in other projections

Plotting the hexagons in another projection moves each of their corners to its new position, so the hexagons stay in place but are stretched with the land beneath them. For example, on a globe centred on Australia:

```{r ortho}
ggplot(ced_hex) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = state)) +
  coord_sf(crs = "+proj=ortho +lat_0=-25 +lon_0=134")
```

The same hexagons in some other projections:

```{r other-projections, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 6}
displays <- list(
  "Albers equal-area (EPSG:3577), as made" = 3577,
  "Globe centred on Australia" = "+proj=ortho +lat_0=-25 +lon_0=134",
  "Longitude and latitude (EPSG:4326)" = 4326,
  "Web Mercator (EPSG:3857)" = 3857
)
wrap_plots(Map(hex_map, list(ced_hex), displays, names(displays)))
```

A globe centred on Australia is close to the Albers projection across the continent, so the hexagons are barely changed. Longitude and latitude shears them, and Web Mercator keeps their shape but enlarges them towards the south.

## Regular hexagons on a globe

On a globe centred away from Australia, the continent is foreshortened towards the horizon, and so are hexagons made in the Albers projection. To have regular hexagons on the plotted map, make them in the projection it will be plotted in.

```{r globe}
globe <- "+proj=ortho +lat_0=0 +lon_0=90"
globe_hex <- hexmap(ced, group = state, crs = globe)
ggplot(globe_hex) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = state))
```

Compared with the Albers hexagons plotted on the same globe:

```{r globe-compare, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 3.5}
hex_map(ced_hex, globe, "Made in EPSG:3577") +
  hex_map(globe_hex, globe, "Made on the globe")
```

The hexagons made on the globe are regular, and tile the outline of Australia as it appears from this viewpoint. The hexagon size, `island_gap`, `group_gap` and the group layouts are all measured in the plane of this projection.

An orthographic globe only shows one hemisphere, so centre it well away from the region. Hexagons on the edge of a region near the horizon may extend past it, where they have no location on the Earth.

## Equally sized hexagons

The hexagons are equally sized in the plane they are made in. They also cover equal areas on the ground when that projection is **equal-area**. Making and plotting the hexagons in an equal-area projection gives hexagons that look regular and represent equal areas, for example:

* an equal-area conic projection for a country or state, such as the Australian Albers (EPSG:3577) or the conterminous United States Albers (EPSG:5070),
* the Lambert azimuthal equal-area projection centred on the region (`"+proj=laea +lat_0=... +lon_0=..."`), which looks like a globe near its centre and is the default for maps in longitude and latitude,
* Equal Earth (`"+proj=eqearth"`) or Mollweide (`"+proj=moll"`) for the whole world.

The orthographic globe is not equal-area, but is close to it near its centre. Web Mercator is far from equal-area. Over Australia, its hexagons cover up to 1.75 times as much ground in the tropical north as in Tasmania.
